entities.name: Abdul Qadir Gilani
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abdul Qadir Gilani, born in Gilan, Persia (modern Iran) around 1077-1078 CE, and died in Baghdad, Iraq, on February 21, 1166, was a towering figure in Islamic spiritual and legal thought. He distinguished himself as a prominent Hanbali scholar, an eloquent preacher, and a profound Sufi mystic, whose teachings laid the foundation for the Qadiriyya, one of the most widespread and enduring Sufi orders globally. His spiritual authority and scholarly depth during the Abbasid Caliphate's twilight years in Baghdad cemented his reputation as a "Sultan al-Awliya" (Sultan of Saints), influencing religious practice and social structure across the Islamic world from West Africa to Southeast Asia.

Gilani's early life saw him migrate to Baghdad in 1095 CE, a vibrant intellectual hub, where he pursued comprehensive studies in Hanbali fiqh (jurisprudence), Hadith, and Quranic exegesis under masters like Abu Sa'id al-Mubarak al-Makhzumi. After a period of intense asceticism and spiritual seclusion, he began to preach publicly around 1127 CE, drawing immense crowds to his madrasa (school) and ribat (Sufi lodge) in Baghdad. His sermons, characterized by their emphasis on strict adherence to the Sharia, personal piety, and repentance, resonated deeply with both the learned elite and the common populace. He authored numerous influential works, including "Al-Fath ar-Rabbani" (The Lordly Opening) and "Futuh al-Ghaib" (Revelations of the Unseen), which encapsulated his spiritual methodology and ethical teachings.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Abdul Qadir Gilani's legacy extends far beyond his lifetime, as his spiritual teachings and the Qadiriyya order he founded influenced the religious landscape of millions across Asia and Africa for centuries. His emphasis on balancing strict adherence to Islamic law with Sufi mysticism helped shape the development of Sunni Islam in numerous regions.
